candidate_findings.message: Non-seekable streams always fail on Android. If the stream can't seek, `length` is `C.LengthUnset` (-1). With an unset `dataSpec.Length`, `bytesRemaining` then becomes `C.LengthUnset`, and the `bytesRemaining < 0` check throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. The code that handles `LengthUnset` in `Read` can never run. The check should exclude `C.LengthUnset`. A past-the-end position should also surface as an IOException/DataSourceException instead of a .NET exception crossing JNI.

Every `StreamDataSource` the factory creates shares one .NET `Stream`, along with its single Position. ExoPlayer may create several data sources and call Open/Read on loader threads, for example when seeking or retrying while an earlier load is still running. Each Open seeks the shared stream, so concurrent or overlapping reads corrupt each other's position and return wrong bytes. Access needs to be serialized (a lock around seek+read), or reads should use per-source offsets.

`currentStreamDataSourceFactory` (a Java.Lang.Object) is disposed before the new source is handed to the player. The old ProgressiveMediaSource may still be loading on ExoPlayer's loader thread with that factory or its data sources. Disposing the managed peer while Java still holds references can cause crashes or ObjectDisposedException in callbacks. CreateMediaItemFromStream (lines ~783-787) has the same problem. The old factory should be released only after SetMediaSource/SetMediaItem has replaced it.

FillDataRequest has three problems. (1) It casts `RequestedLength` to int and allocates a buffer that big. AVFoundation often asks for the whole resource (or sets RequestsAllDataToEndOfResource), so this can allocate the entire media size at once or overflow for files over 2 GB. (2) It calls `Stream.Read` only once and ignores short reads, but `ShouldWaitForLoadingOfRequestedResource` still calls `FinishLoading()`. A stream that returns fewer bytes than requested (FileStream, network or decrypting streams) gives AVPlayer truncated data. (3) Exceptions are caught and only logged, then `FinishLoading()` reports success instead of `FinishLoadingWithError`, so the failure never reaches MediaFailed. Data should be served in chunks in a loop, honoring RequestsAllDataToEndOfResource, and errors should be reported.

For non-seekable streams, ContentLength is set to 0. AVFoundation treats that as an empty resource, so playback fails, and nothing reports this to the caller. Either reject or document non-seekable streams on Apple platforms, or buffer them.

GetStreamContentType only returns `public.mpeg-4` or QuickTime, so audio streams (MP3, M4A, WAV, etc.) get the wrong UTI. That contradicts the 'works with both audio and video' claim. It also duplicates the new shared `StreamExtensions.GetMimeType` sniffer instead of reusing it (mapped to UTIs). It doesn't catch IO/NotSupported exceptions, which then escape PlatformUpdateSource. And the `Length: > 12` check plus the duplicated `"public.mpeg-4"` literal at the end should be cleaned up.

`AsRandomAccessStream()` throws NotSupportedException for non-seekable streams. Nothing catches it here, so a valid StreamMediaSource crashes the app instead of raising MediaFailed. This branch also sets `Player.Source` while every other branch uses `Player.MediaPlayer.Set*Source`. The created IRandomAccessStream / MediaSource is never disposed when the source changes.

Throwing NotSupportedException from PlatformUpdateSource fires inside the Source property-changed pipeline, so on Tizen setting a StreamMediaSource crashes the app. The usual pattern is to log and raise MediaFailed / set the Failed state. If the Stream is null, the branch silently does nothing.

The sniffing heuristics are too loose. Any stream whose first byte is 0x47 (e.g. 'G', as in GIF) is labelled `video/mp2t`. The 0xFFEx/0xFFFx sync check also matches AAC ADTS (0xFFF1/0xFFF9), which gets reported as `audio/mpeg`. A wrong MIME type passed to `CreateFromStream` can make Windows playback fail. TS detection should check for 0x47 at 188-byte intervals, and ADTS should be excluded (layer bits == 00).
The XML doc says these are extensions 'on Windows platform', but the file is `.shared.cs` and compiled for every target. Meanwhile macios has its own duplicate sniffer.

OnAppearing is `async void`, and `httpClient.GetStreamAsync` runs outside any try/catch. With no network, or on an HTTP error, the exception is unhandled and crashes the sample app. The 30 MB download into a MemoryStream also repeats on every appearance, including after returning from the media picker, which replaces the video the user just picked or recorded.

OnDisappearing disposes the MemoryStream while MediaElement.Source still points at it and the native player may still be reading it on a background thread. That causes ObjectDisposedException on the loader/resource-loader thread. Opening the MediaPicker also triggers OnDisappearing, which kills the current stream. The sample should clear `MediaElement.Source` (and stop playback) before disposing the stream, since this is exactly the lifetime pattern users will copy.

UpdateSourceStream assigns `sourceStream` outside the semaphore, while ReleaseSourceStream checks `sourceStream is null` before acquiring it. Concurrent calls (the OnAppearing download racing a picker result) can leak or double-dispose streams. Also, in ReleaseSourceStream (~line 261), `WaitAsync` sits inside the try, so if it throws, `finally` releases a semaphore that was never acquired.

ConvertTo for StreamMediaSource returns a string like 'Stream: MemoryStream'. Converting that back yields a bogus Uri/File source, so the converter no longer round-trips. A Stream can't be represented as a string, so this case should return string.Empty, as the base MediaSource case does, or not be convertible at all.

If the install method is "git" but `dist/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh` is missing, this code quietly switches to a global `npm install -g @aoagents/ao@latest`. That can happen when the CLI was built with plain `tsc` or `tsc --watch`, because those skip the `cp -r src/assets dist/` step. The npm install then overwrites the `npm link` launcher with a published package and leaves the checkout itself unchanged. The method is also hardcoded to "npm-global", so pnpm and bun users get the wrong command. A source checkout with a missing script is a build problem, so it should fail with a clear error (for example, "run pnpm build") instead of changing how AO is installed.

The ao-specific marker (`scripts/ao-update.sh`) was removed from the check, so any non-node_modules path whose fourth parent directory has a `.git` is now classified as a "git" source install, even when it isn't an AO checkout. `ao update` would then run the source-update flow (git pull, pnpm build) against the wrong repo, or fall into the npm fallback above. Check for an AO-specific marker instead, such as `packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh` or the `packages/ao` directory.

The default `REPO_ROOT` is still `$(dirname BASH_SOURCE)/..`. That was correct when the script lived at `scripts/`, but after the move it resolves to `packages/cli/src/assets` (or `dist/assets`). Anyone who runs the script directly without `AO_REPO_ROOT` set will get a wrong root, and its git, pnpm and npm link steps will fail or act on the wrong directory. It needs to go up 4 levels, or the fallback should be removed and `AO_REPO_ROOT` required.

After the move, the default `REPO_ROOT` (`dirname/..`) points to `assets/` rather than the repo or package root. Layout detection then reports `source-checkout`, and when the script runs without `AO_REPO_ROOT` every repo check is made against the wrong directory, which produces false failures.

The regex escape is wrong. `/[.*+?^${}()|[\\]\\\\]/g` is a character class followed by literal backslashes, so it almost never matches and the path is effectively inserted unescaped. The test passes only because `.` happens to match itself. A checkout path containing characters such as `+`, `(` or `[` would make the test fail or throw. Use the standard `/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g`.

The package-install path does not use `$REPO_ROOT/packages`, but the fix hint for a source checkout (`bash scripts/setup.sh`) is still tied to a root-level `scripts/` directory. Now that the AO scripts have moved out of root `scripts/`, check that `setup.sh` still exists there, or the hint will point users to a missing file.

`saveScheduled` is now reset in `finally`, after the storage put finishes. Before this change it was reset at the start of the timer callback. Any `scheduleSave()` call that arrives while the put is running now returns early, so updates received during the write are never scheduled for saving. If no later update comes in and the Durable Object is evicted, those updates are lost. Reset the flag before taking the snapshot, or reschedule in `finally` when the buffer changed during the write.

The new per-partition debounce has the same lost-update window. `saveScheduled` stays true until the put finishes, so `trackUpdate` calls during the write skip scheduling. Those updates sit unsaved until another update reaches the same partition. Clear the flag before reading `partitionUpdates`, or reschedule in `finally` when new updates arrived during the write.

`applyClientUpdate` returns true when `doc` is null. The doc is only created lazily (by thumbnail/snapshot requests), so most of the time no validation happens and corrupt updates are still pushed, tracked, broadcast and saved. The new `if (!applied) break` guard in board-room.ts therefore only works some of the time. This server change is also missing from the PR description, which covers only rotation.

Double-click edit detection calls the raw, non-rotation-aware `hitTest` directly instead of the wrapped one. On a rotated text shape, the click that the select tool counts as a hit (via `withRotation`) can miss here, and clicks outside the visible shape can start editing. Use the same `withRotation(hitTest)` here.
Same problem as in the text plugin: the sticky double-click/edit path uses the unwrapped `hitTest`, so editing a rotated sticky ignores its rotation and disagrees with selection hit-testing.

`ShapeWrapper` now visually rotates every shape type, but only the basic, image, text, wireframe and sticky `hitTest`s were wrapped. Freedraw, counter, board-portal, connector, frame, group, island, community-chat and community-region still hit-test against unrotated bounds. A rotated shape of those types draws in one place but is clickable in another. Either wrap them too or only apply the CSS rotation to types that support it.

Marquee selection (and the selection overlay/resize handles) use `def.getBounds(data)`, which still ignores rotation. The spatial index now uses the rotated AABB, so the two disagree: marquee in contain mode may wrongly include or exclude rotated shapes, and the overlay is drawn at the unrotated box. A rotation-aware `getBounds` (or `getRotatedAABB` here) is needed for consistency.
Thumbnail generation drops `rotation` when it copies shape data, so server thumbnails show rotated shapes unrotated and no longer match the canvas.

The 'safety net' in the SMP vTaskSwitchContext() blocks every context switch while the current task has xPreemptionDisable set, including switches the task asks for itself. vTaskPreemptionDisable() is only meant to stop preemption. A task with preemption disabled can still block (vTaskDelay, a blocking queue/semaphore/notify wait), call taskYIELD(), suspend itself, or delete itself. In each of those cases the task has already been taken off the ready list, but vTaskSwitchContext() now only sets xYieldPendings and returns, so the task keeps running. A blocked task that keeps running ignores its timeout and ends up using a stale wait result, and a suspended or deleted task keeps executing on its own TCB/stack. This is not like the uxSchedulerSuspended case it copies: blocking APIs already refuse to run while the scheduler is suspended, but nothing stops a preemption-disabled task from blocking. prvSelectHighestPriorityTask() already keeps a running, ready, preemption-disabled task in place, so this check is unnecessary and should be removed, or limited to switches that are not voluntary.

Reporting a yield only on a pdFALSE->pdTRUE change of xYieldPendings throws away valid yield requests. If xYieldPendings[core] is already pdTRUE for a valid reason, such as a time-slice or yield deferred inside a critical section, or an earlier FromISR call whose caller passed NULL or ignored the result, then resuming a higher-priority task for this core no longer sets xYieldRequired. The ISR then skips portYIELD_FROM_ISR and the switch waits until the next tick or kernel call. That is a latency regression and changes the documented return contract. This hunk only treats the symptom; the actual bug is the stale flag that the tick-path change fixes.

Same before/after check in xTaskRemoveFromEventList(). This function is also called from task context in queue, event-group and stream-buffer code. If a yield was already pending on this core, it now returns pdFALSE even when the unblocked task should preempt the caller. The queueYIELD_IF_USING_PREEMPTION or *pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken path is then skipped and the higher-priority task does not get the CPU right away.

In xTaskGenericNotifyFromISR, the check means *pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken is not set when xYieldPendings was already pdTRUE, for example from an earlier notify in the same ISR whose caller passed NULL. In that case the ISR never calls portYIELD_FROM_ISR, even though the notified task has higher priority than the task running on this core. vTaskGenericNotifyGiveFromISR at lines 8351-8364 has the same problem.

The PR says the change only affects configUSE_TASK_PREEMPTION_DISABLE == 1 builds, but the pdFALSE->pdTRUE yield checks in xTaskResumeFromISR, xTaskRemoveFromEventList and both notify-from-ISR functions are compiled into every SMP build with preemption enabled. That changes yield-reporting behaviour for all SMP users, including those who never use vTaskPreemptionDisable. The existing SMP unit tests also check that these functions return a yield request, and the test plan does not cover this.

The ENTROPY expression calls `.otherwise(...)` on the result of `F.sum(...)`. PySpark only allows `.otherwise()` on a Column built by `F.when()`, so `F.sum(F.when(...)).otherwise(...)` raises at runtime. Any pipeline with an ENTROPY metric fails when the script runs, even though `ast.parse` accepts it. The `.otherwise(F.lit(0.0))` belongs inside the `F.sum(...)`, or should be dropped.

MODE is generated as `F.first(category, ignorenulls=True)`, which returns an arbitrary category from each group, not the dominant one. It should return the category with the largest `<agg>_cat_val`, for example `F.max_by(cat, cat_val)` or `F.max(F.struct(cat_val, cat))[cat]`. As written the feature is non-deterministic and semantically wrong.
RATIO is generated as a plain windowed sum, which gives the same value as SUM_U. No ratio is computed. These features would be silently mislabeled duplicates.

PROM_P generates the same expression as PROM_U, and SUM_P the same as SUM_U. The enum and the output contracts treat them as different operators, so the `_P` variants come out as redundant copies of the `_U` features under different names instead of their intended semantics.

XM generates the same expression as FREQ: a count of non-null values in the window. If XM means something different, every XM feature is a duplicate of FREQ. The operator's semantics need confirming and implementing.

CREC ignores `window_size`. It always compares against `lag(1)`, so CREC features with different windows (for example 3 and 6) come out identical. CREC is also allowed on TEMPORAL (FECHA) columns by TemporalOutputContract, and subtracting and dividing date columns fails at runtime.

MEDIA_ABS is generated as a windowed approximate median (`percentile_approx(..., 0.5)`). The operator name ('media' means mean) and its pairing with RATIO under `composed_windows` suggest a composed metric such as mean absolute deviation, not a median. This needs confirming against the spec, and the median is approximate in any case.

Categorical values are interpolated into the generated code as `"{cat_val}"` without escaping. A value containing a double quote or backslash produces broken or injectable Python, and numeric categories are compared as strings. Use `{cat_val!r}` or `F.lit(...)` with proper quoting, as the code already does for table names.

`frame_w` is only assigned when `w is not None`. Windowed operators currently always have a `window_size`, but any future operator or override that reaches a `frame_w` branch without one raises `UnboundLocalError` instead of a clear error. Also, the `col_ref` conditional on lines 300-304 produces the same expression on both branches, so it is dead logic.

`generate()` narrows its return type from `FeatureStoreOutput` to `object`, which breaks the base-class contract for type checkers. It also relies on `assert` for runtime type checks, and asserts are removed under `python -O`. It would be cleaner to override `_combine_code` and prepend the header there, or keep the `FeatureStoreOutput` return annotation.

The header imports `SparkSession` but never creates `spark`, while the rest of the script uses `spark` throughout. Outside a Databricks notebook the script fails with a NameError. Either add `spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` or drop the unused import.

The tests only check `ast.parse` and substring presence, so runtime-invalid PySpark (the ENTROPY `.otherwise` bug) and wrong semantics (MODE, RATIO, duplicate operators) pass. Asserting the expression generated for each operator and metric, or running against a local SparkSession, would catch these.

`this.eventService.isRegistered(...)` is async, and its result is used here without `await`. A Promise is always truthy, so `!promise` is always false and the registration check never runs. Staff can check in anyone who isn't registered for the event.

`User.findBy` can return null, for example if a participant profile has no linked user. The code then uses the `user!` non-null assertion and goes on to read `user.id`, which throws a TypeError and returns a 500 instead of a clean error. Handle a null user explicitly.

`eventID` is taken from the request body without validation. If it is missing or invalid, `findOrFail` throws a 404 or 500 instead of returning a user-facing error. Validate it with a validator, or put the event id in the route params as other event routes do (`/:id/...`).

The check-in route uses only `middleware.staff()` and has no `middleware.auth()` before it. `StaffMiddleware` calls `ctx.auth.getUserOrFail()`, which fails unless the user was authenticated earlier. Unauthenticated requests therefore error out instead of being redirected to login. Add `middleware.auth()`, as the register route does.

The route is `/events/:slug/check-in`: the participant slug sits where every other route in this group has the event id, and the event id travels in the body. This is confusing, and a slug could clash with other `/:id/...` patterns. Prefer `/events/:id/check-in/:slug`.

This breaks the Rules of Hooks. `useTuyau` and `useForm` are called after a conditional early return (`if (!isOpen) return null`), so the number of hooks changes when `isOpen` toggles and React throws 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'. The parent always mounts this component and only toggles `isOpen`, so opening the dialog will crash.

The scanner uses `allowMultiple={true}` and `scanDelay={0}`, and the dialog stays open until the request succeeds. One QR code held in front of the camera fires many `onScan` callbacks, each sending a check-in POST. These race and produce spurious 'already checked-in' errors or unique-constraint 500s. Debounce, or ignore scans while a request is processing.

The check-in is check-then-insert: `isCheckedIn` runs, then `attach` runs, with nothing tying them together. Concurrent requests (likely, given the multi-scan behaviour) can both pass the check, and the second insert then hits the unique constraint with an unhandled DB error. Also, `event.save()` is pointless here because nothing on the event was modified.

The QR check-in trigger is inside the `{!isRegistered && ...}` block, so a staff member who is registered for the event never sees it. It is also a bare `QrCode` SVG with an `onClick`, so keyboard and screen-reader users can't reach it. Move it out of that block and wrap it in a `Button`.

`event_id` and `user_id` are nullable and have no `onDelete` behaviour. Pivot rows can exist with null keys, and deleting an event or user will be blocked by FK violations. Make both columns `notNullable()` and add `onDelete('CASCADE')`. The file name also repeats 'create_create'.

This seeder has no `.dev` suffix or environment guard, so it runs with every `db:seed` in every environment and silently gives user id 1 a staff profile. It also creates the StaffProfile without a department, which will fail if `department_id` is required. Restrict it to dev or remove it.

`Department.create({ id: 99 })` hard-codes a primary key. It is not idempotent, so re-seeding fails, and on Postgres it does not advance the sequence, so a later insert can collide. It also runs outside dev, creating a staff account with the password 'password'.

The shell `if` has two `else` branches: one at line 41 and another at line 94, followed by a single `fi`. That is a bash syntax error. The `run:` script fails to parse before any branch runs, so every trigger fails at this step: `workflow_run`, dispatch with a `run_id`, and dispatch without one. This looks like a leftover from an incomplete merge. The first block, which has no 7-day window, should be removed and only the newer fallback kept.

The 'Resolve source workflow run ID' step has the `env:` mapping twice. YAML does not allow duplicate keys, and GitHub Actions rejects the workflow file with an invalid-workflow error, so the workflow never starts.

The heredocs inside the `else` branches are indented 2 spaces deeper than the rest of the `run:` block. YAML strips only the common indentation, so the closing `PY` lines keep their leading spaces. `<<'PY'` (not `<<-`) only ends at a column-0 `PY`, so neither heredoc terminates. Python would also get indented code and raise `IndentationError: unexpected indent`. Even after the duplicate `else` is fixed, the no-`run_id` dispatch path would still fail.

With the `head_branch` filter gone, any successful 'Weekly Grype Security Scan' run on any branch or event now rewrites the single tracking issue. That includes manual runs on feature branches and PR-triggered runs, if that workflow has such triggers. The issue can be overwritten with results from an unrelated branch, and possibly from attacker-influenced artifacts, using an `issues: write` token. Filter on something reliable instead: `workflow_run.event == 'schedule'`, or a branch marker written into the artifact.
`${{ inputs.run_id }}` is substituted directly into the shell script, which lets the dispatch input inject shell commands. Pass it through `env:` and validate that it is numeric before using it.
When the latest scan has no fixable recommendations, the issue step is skipped. Any existing tracking issue keeps showing stale recommendations instead of being updated or closed.

`github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]'` checks who triggered this particular event, not who opened the PR. If a maintainer re-runs the job, or pushes to or rebases the Dependabot PR, the job is skipped and reported as passing. The regression gate is then bypassed without any warning. Use `github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]'` instead.

`underfixed_updates` fails any changed package that still has a fixable High/Critical finding, even when the PR fixes that finding and introduces no new High/Critical vulnerability. Packages are tracked by name only, so a package that appears in several layers or ecosystems can also be marked as 'changed' or 'underfixed' incorrectly. Nothing checks whether the fix version is actually newer than the PR's version, or whether base already had the same unfixed finding. As a result, partial upgrades that still improve security are blocked, and the step summary never lists the underfixed packages to explain the failure.
`recs = fixed_recommendations(pr)` is calculated twice (lines 159 and 173). This is dead or duplicated code left over from the refactor.

The Grype image is resolved from 'releases/latest' at runtime and isn't pinned to a tag or digest. It then runs with `/var/run/docker.sock` mounted, which is root-equivalent on the runner. A compromised or broken upstream release would run immediately with that access, and gate results can't be reproduced. The GitHub API call is also unauthenticated, so it can hit rate limits. Pin the version or digest and let Dependabot update it.

This changes the Dependabot schedule from 06:00 to 09:30 for all ecosystems, but the PR description doesn't mention it. If the time is meant to line up with the weekly Grype scan, document that dependency. Otherwise, revert it.

`ownerName`, `email` and `phone` were removed from `prepareForValidation` and `validationMapping`, but `companySchema` (src/lib/schemas.ts:153) still requires `ownerName` (min 2 chars). Validating an edited company will therefore always fail on an empty `ownerName`. Because `ownerName` is no longer in `validationMapping`, that error has no field to show on, so Save is blocked with no visible reason. Update `companySchema` to match the new `Company` shape (drop `ownerName`/`email`/`phone`, add `description`).

The creation form no longer has an Owner Name field, but it is still validated against `companySchema`, which requires `ownerName`. Creating a company can never pass validation. The schema needs to be updated together with these form fields.

`location` is still an editable plain-text field, but its value is now a raw WKT string such as `POINT(lon lat)`. Users would have to hand-type WKT, and anything else they enter will just display as text and break the map link. Make it read-only, or add a proper map/coordinate picker (the `renderer` hook).

The map-link branch is triggered for any entity that has a field with key `location`, not just companies. It also reads `data[field.key]`, not the edited value that `getFieldValue` uses, so after an inline save the link opens the old coordinates. Use an explicit field type or renderer (e.g. `type: 'wktPoint'`) and read from the same source as the other fields.

`parseWKTPoint`'s regex `[\d.\-]+` accepts malformed numbers like `1-2` (parseFloat silently turns that into 1). It also rejects valid forms such as `+` signs, exponent notation and `POINT Z (...)`. The function runs on every render and has no tests.

`on:keydown|stopPropagation` on the focusable dialog (tabindex=0) stops keydown events from bubbling to the `svelte:window` handler. Once focus is inside the modal (e.g. after clicking it), pressing Escape no longer closes it. Remove the `stopPropagation` on keydown, or handle Escape on the dialog itself.

When the API gives no total, `totalItems` is set to `fetchedCount + 1` whenever a page is full. Pagination then only ever offers one page beyond the current one, and the final page can come back empty, which forces a second request through the recursive step-back. Prefer having the backend return a total count, or use a simple next/previous control.

The table shows IDs as `COMP-<id>` and the search placeholder says users can search by ID. However, the search term goes straight to the backend `search` param, so typing the displayed `COMP-12` probably won't match. Either strip the prefix and send it as `id`, or don't advertise ID search.
The spinner overlay has a hard-coded white translucent background (`rgba(255,255,255,0.5)`), while the rest of the UI uses theme variables. It will flash white in dark mode.
The `.location-display` CSS rule is never used. Svelte will report an unused-selector warning.

The notebook calls `wg_fin.run_inference(...)`, but `financial_impact/financial.py` has no such function. The cell raises AttributeError and is re-raised, so the pipeline cannot run. The module docstring says inference was deliberately left out, so the committed outputs must come from different code that isn't in this change.
The artifacts branch also calls the missing `wg_fin.run_inference`, so it fails the same way.

`wg_fin.load_artifacts` is not defined in `financial.py`. The broad `except Exception` catches the AttributeError and prints "No artifacts.pkl", which hides the bug. As written, the artifacts path can never run.

`from financial_impact import financial` runs before `repo_root` is added to `sys.path`. The notebook lives in `wafer_images/`, so the import fails unless the kernel was started at the repo root. `repo_root` is also hardcoded to one developer's home directory (`/Users/hernanmontoyag/...`), so the notebook won't work on any other machine and the commit leaks a local path.

The committed outputs are stale and don't match this code. They show en-dash yield ranges ("18%–85%") where the code produces hyphens, and the cell's `execution_count` is null. Readers will be misled about what the library produces. Clear the outputs or re-run the notebook with the committed code.

`compute_financials` accepts a `financial_params` override, but `get_params` always reads the module-level `FINANCIAL_PARAMS`, so the argument is silently ignored. Callers such as a Streamlit app that pass custom cost tables will get the default numbers.

`dt_cost = params['dt'] * repair_hours` treats `dt` as a cost per hour. With values like 2,050,000 × 8 that's about $16M of downtime per repair, which dominates EVoA and makes most patterns negative (see the notebook output). Check the unit of `dt` (per hour vs. per event or day). If the unit is wrong, the recommendations will be wrong.

`decode_labels` maps any unknown class ID to "00000000" (Normal). A mapping mismatch would silently count defective wafers as passing, which understates the defect rate and the financial loss. Unknown IDs should raise an error or be flagged.
The summary `avg_confidence` is an unweighted mean of per-pattern averages, so a pattern with 3 wafers counts as much as one with 5,000. Use the mean over all wafers, or weight by count.

`dominant_pattern` takes the first non-normal row of `df_batch`. That's only correct if the input is sorted by count descending, which `compute_financials` doesn't enforce. Use `idxmax` on `count` instead.
For combinations, replacement costs with `replace=None` (e.g. Random) are skipped silently. The combined replacement cost then understates the real cost without saying so.
`int(params['ylo'] * 100)` truncates float products, so some values display one percent low (e.g. 0.29*100 = 28.999… shows as 28%). Use `round()`.
The output key is hardcoded as `evoa_30d`, but the value uses the configurable `PLANNING_HORIZON`. If the horizon changes, the key mislabels the metric.

This change removes the ignore rules for `PresentationPDFs/` and `architecture_report.pdf`, which looks unintended and lets large binary PDFs be committed. It also adds `requirements.txt` to `.gitignore`, which keeps a dependency file out of version control; CI already has an 'Install requirements' step. Only one generated report JSON is ignored, while the CSVs written to the same directory are not.

The 'batch' is the entire dataset, including training samples, so the reported defect rate and losses describe the training distribution, not a production lot. Label it as a demo, or use held-out or real lot data.

There is no `--apple-api-key-id` option, and `appleApiKeyId` is declared as a local `undefined` (line 53) and never set from options. Because of this, API Key auth for iOS can never work in a non-interactive environment such as CI: the command always fails with 'You must provide the Apple API Key ID…', even when `--apple-api-key-file` and `--apple-issuer-id` are passed. The non-interactive error message at line 212 tells users that those two flags are enough, which is wrong. Add an `appleApiKeyId` option and include it in the auth-method detection.

The .p8 Apple API key is uploaded to the server before the Key ID, Issuer ID and Team ID are collected and checked. If any later step fails (a non-interactive missing flag, an empty prompt, or Ctrl+C), the private key is left uploaded with nothing using it. Collect and check every input first, then upload the key just before creating the destination.

Provisioning profiles are uploaded before the certificate is created and linked to it afterwards. If certificate creation fails (for example a wrong password or an invalid file) or `updateMany` fails, the uploaded profiles are left orphaned and nothing is rolled back or reported. The certificate file is also read only after all prompts, so a mistyped path ends in an unhandled ENOENT stack trace instead of a clear error. Check that all file paths exist up front and create the certificate before uploading the profiles, or clean up on failure.

Provisioning profiles passed with `--provisioning-profile` are uploaded and linked whatever the platform is, including android and web, where they make no sense. Only the interactive prompt checks for iOS. Reject this flag or ignore it when the platform is not ios.

`provisioningProfile` is defined as `z.array(z.string())`, but no other command uses an array option. If zli passes a single `--provisioning-profile path` as a plain string, Zod validation fails and the documented flag is unusable. Check how zli parses repeated or single flags, or accept `z.union([z.string(), z.array(z.string())])` and normalize it.
The certificate password and key password are prompted with `type: 'text'`, so the secrets are echoed on screen and stay in terminal scrollback and screen recordings. Use a masked or password input.
The Apple app-specific password is prompted with `type: 'text'`, so the secret is echoed on screen. Use a masked input.

`AppDestinationDto` includes `appleAppPassword`, and `get` prints the whole object with `console.table` or JSON. If the API returns this field, the command prints the app-specific password in plain text. Leave secret fields out of the output.

`promptAppSelection` now loads at most 50 apps and has no pagination or search. This affects every command that uses app selection, not just the new ones. In organizations with more than 50 apps, some apps silently disappear from the picker, and the user cannot select them interactively.

Delete by `--name`/`--platform` takes the first result of `findAll({ name })` without checking that the name matches exactly or that there is only one match. If the server's `name` filter matches partially, case-insensitively (note `nameLower`) or returns several rows, the wrong certificate can be deleted, and with `--yes` there is no confirmation. Require exactly one exact match. The same pattern is in `destinations/delete.ts`.

In interactive mode, a `--name` given without `--platform` is silently ignored and the user gets the full picker. The picker also calls `findAll` without a limit, so it only shows the server's default page and some certificates may not be selectable. The same applies to `get.ts` and the destination delete and get commands.

The interactively entered certificate ID is not checked, so an empty answer becomes a PATCH to `/certificates/`. Nothing checks that at least one field to update was given either, so the command sends an empty PATCH and still reports 'Certificate updated successfully.' Unlike `delete` and `get`, this command also cannot pick a certificate from a list. `destinations/update.ts` has the same problems.

`update` asks for raw server IDs (`--app-apple-api-key-id`, `--app-google-service-account-key-id`), but no command lists or creates those keys on their own. `create` only accepts key file paths. This makes it practically impossible to rotate a destination's key with the CLI. Accept file paths here and upload them, as `create` does.

`CreateAppProvisioningProfileDto.certificateId` is never set by any caller. It is also named inconsistently with the `appCertificateId` field used elsewhere for the same API, so the service would probably send a form field the API does not recognize. Remove it or rename it to `appCertificateId`.

Nothing on the CoreSync server checks authorization. UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization only fill in HttpContext.User. No endpoint or middleware calls RequireAuthorization, and the RequireSyncReadWrite policy is registered but never used. So with Auth:UseEntraId=true, a request with no token, an expired token or a forged token still reaches UseCoreSyncHttpServer() and can read or write the whole sync database. Calling this 'Bearer token on the sync client' with 'JWT Bearer validation' suggests the channel is protected when it is not. Add a gate before UseCoreSyncHttpServer() that returns a challenge when the user is not authenticated or lacks sync.readwrite, at least when UseEntraId is true.

Auth fails open. Auth:UseEntraId defaults to false when the setting is missing, and it is only set in appsettings.Development.json (appsettings.json is gitignored). In any non-Development deployment, DevAuthHandler therefore signs in every anonymous caller as 'dev-user'/'dev-tenant'. The same is true of the API. Default to Entra ID outside Development, or refuse to register DevAuthHandler unless app.Environment.IsDevelopment().

AppHost hardcodes Auth__UseEntraId="false" for the API. Any azd/Aspire deployment built from this AppHost will run the API with DevAuthHandler in production. The 'web' (CoreSync) project gets no Auth/AzureAd environment variables, so turning on Entra ID for it would fail at startup: the AzureAd section is missing outside Development because appsettings.json is gitignored. Make the flag a parameter that differs per environment, and pass the same AzureAd values to the web project.

Short claim names like "tid" and "oid" will usually be null for real Entra tokens. JwtBearer (and AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi) keep MapInboundClaims=true by default, which renames tid to http://schemas.microsoft.com/identity/claims/tenantid and oid to http://schemas.microsoft.com/identity/claims/objectidentifier. In production TenantId would then fall back to a 'tenant_id' claim that Entra never issues, so it is null. UserId would fall back to NameIdentifier, which is mapped from the pairwise 'sub', not the oid. Tenant and user isolation would break. Use ClaimsPrincipal.GetObjectId()/GetTenantId() from Microsoft.Identity.Web, check the full URI claim types too, or set MapInboundClaims=false.

The test token carries both the Entra claims (tid/oid) and the DevAuthHandler claims (tenant_id, NameIdentifier, ClaimTypes.Name/Email). API_ExtractsTenantContext passes through the fallback claims even though inbound claim mapping renames tid/oid. The test hides the claim-mapping bug in TenantContextMiddleware. Emit only the claims a real Entra access token has (tid, oid, name, preferred_username, scp).

This factory leaves Auth:UseEntraId=false, so DevAuthHandler is still registered. It then adds a plain AddJwtBearer scheme over the top. The production branch (AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi plus the RequireScope policies) never runs in tests, so the tests cannot show that 'Auth:UseEntraId=true' works as the docs claim. Set Auth:UseEntraId=true and override the Microsoft.Identity.Web JwtBearerOptions (for example with PostConfigure on the Bearer scheme) instead.

The test hosts use the API's real Program setup, which puts the database at ApplicationData/sentencestudio/server/sentencestudio.db. That is the developer's real server database, shared with the Web sync server. Integration tests can therefore open, migrate or change real user data, which goes against the repo's data-preservation rules. Swap AddDataServices for a temporary or in-memory database in the test factories.
The new test project is not added to src/SentenceStudio.sln, so 'dotnet test' on the solution and CI will not run these tests.

Email falls back to 'preferred_username'. That is a UPN or sign-in name that users can sometimes change, not a verified email address, and it can be a phone number or a non-mail UPN. Treating it as Email can mislabel identities. Use the 'email' claim (with the optional claim configured), or leave Email null.

`_AndroidRunNativeCompile` now has DependsOnTargets=`_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems`, but that target is only defined in Microsoft.Android.Sdk.TypeMap.LlvmIr.targets. Xamarin.Android.Common.targets imports that file only when `_AndroidTypeMapImplementation != 'trimmable'`. NativeAOT supports the trimmable typemap (there is a Microsoft.Android.Sdk.TypeMap.Trimmable.NativeAOT.targets), and in that configuration the build fails with MSB4057 (target does not exist). Define the target where both typemaps can see it (for example in the designer or common targets), or hook it in with BeforeTargets/AfterTargets instead of a hard DependsOnTargets.

The prelink copies are added to FileWrites only through the task's ModifiedAssemblies output. When the target is skipped as up to date (stamp newer than its inputs), the task doesn't run, so `_PreTrimmingModifiedAssembly` is empty and no FileWrites are added. IncrementalClean then treats `$(IntermediateOutputPath)prelink/*.dll` (listed in FileListAbsolute by the previous build) as orphaned and deletes them. The stamp is kept (Common.targets adds `$(_AndroidStampDirectory)*.stamp` to FileWrites), so later builds keep skipping the task, `_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems` finds no prelink files, and the original libraries go to ILLink. Their designer fields are no longer rooted because the descriptor was removed, and are never redirected to the designer assembly, so resource IDs are wrong or missing at runtime. Always add `$(IntermediateOutputPath)prelink/**` to FileWrites, for example in the UpdateItems target or a target that is never skipped.

The swap replaces any ResolvedFileToPublish .dll that has a same-named file in the prelink directory, not just the assemblies this build produced. Old prelink files are never removed, so stale copies get used. Example: a library is upgraded to a version that no longer needs rewriting (or the task now leaves it alone); the old rewritten copy from an earlier build is still swapped in, which publishes outdated library code. Matching by filename only also ignores the item's original path. Swap only items backed by a manifest of the current outputs (for example, write the modified list to a file next to the stamp and read it back), and clear the prelink directory before the task writes.

Incrementality relies only on timestamps: Inputs=@(_PreTrimmingAssembly) against a single stamp. Adding or upgrading a package reference whose extracted assembly has an mtime older than the stamp (NuGet keeps package entry timestamps) won't rerun the task. A new library is then trimmed without having its Resource field loads rewritten (resource IDs are wrong at runtime). An upgraded library is replaced by the stale prelink copy of the old version. Add a hash or list of the input paths to the inputs (for example, write the item list to a file with WriteOnlyWhenDifferent and include that file in Inputs).

The change adds a new task, a stamp-based target and an item-swapping target, but the only test changes are updated apkdesc size baselines. No tests cover incremental builds (a second build with no changes, adding or upgrading a library, IncrementalClean) or a library with a legacy designer actually running against the trimmed designer assembly. Those are the scenarios most likely to break, as the issues above show.

The staleness check can never find a fresh plan. Phase 4.1 writes the tasks file, then Phase 4.5 rewrites the story file (Section 8.1). That leaves mtime(story) > mtime(tasks) after every run, so each later run counts as stale (rule at lines 97-104) and launches all 5 agents again. The idempotency rule (RULE-002) is broken. Fix: write or touch the tasks file after the story update, or base staleness on something other than the story's mtime.

DoR checks 1 (architecture plan) and 9 (implementation plan) require a file with layer analysis or a component list. Phase 4 never writes the Architect's architecture or implementation plan to disk; it only writes tasks, task plans, the report and the DoR file. Unless x-dev-architecture-plan or x-dev-lifecycle ran earlier, these checks can only be answered from transient agent output, so the result depends on how the model reads the instructions. Persist the Architect's plans (e.g. architecture-story-XXXX-YYYY.md and plan-story-XXXX-YYYY.md) in Phase 4, or define the check against the planning report.

On reuse, the skill jumps to Phase 5 without invoking any subagent. Checks 2, 3, 11 and 12 are defined against 'QA agent output', 'Security agent output' or an existing tests/security file. On the reuse path no agent output exists and those files usually don't either, so reuse either returns NOT_READY spuriously or cannot be evaluated. The QA and Security outputs need to be persisted (e.g. in the planning report) and the checks should read from there.

The TPP ordering contradicts itself. The QA prompt numbers Level 4 = conditional and Level 5 = collection. The proposal enum (line 200), the ordering rule in 3.3 (line 494) and planning-guide.md put collection before conditional. DoR check 2 asks for 'TPP level ordering (1 through 6)', so QA output that follows its own prompt can be judged out of order. Use one canonical sequence everywhere.

The final ordering puts every RED task first (all TPP levels and layers), then every GREEN task. That turns Red-Green-Refactor into 'write all failing tests up front', which conflicts with the incremental TDD cycles required by Rule 03/05 and with the PAIR intent of a RED immediately before its GREEN. Order by RED/GREEN/REFACTOR cycle, not by phase bucket.

The MERGE rule (same component and same layer from different agents, merged into one task) also matches QA RED/GREEN tasks and the Architect's GREEN task for the same class. Example: QA-001 RED for UserValidator merged with ARCH-003 GREEN for UserValidator. The result is one task holding test-writing and implementation DoD, which destroys the RED/GREEN pairing. A GREEN that depended on the merged RED then depends on itself. Restrict MERGE to tasks with the same tdd_phase/type.

The implicit 'all domain tasks before all application tasks before all adapter tasks' dependencies apply to every task, including RED tests and SEC/TL VERIFY tasks. They will conflict with explicit dependencies, e.g. a domain-layer SEC verify task that depends on an application-layer ARCH task. The result is spurious cycles, which hit the 'abort on circular dependency' path. Limit implicit layer edges to GREEN implementation tasks.

The `type` enum (architecture|test|security|quality-gate|validation) has no `implementation` value. Section 3.1 (line 425) lists 'implementation' as an expected Architect type, and AUGMENT (line 449) keys on 'implementation task (from Architect)'. Consolidation rules that depend on the type are therefore ambiguous.

Rule 5 says PO amendments are applied to the story's acceptance criteria section. Phase 4.5 only describes updating Section 8, and planning-guide.md says the amendments are captured in PO tasks. Rewriting the story's Gherkin also lets PO-added scenarios satisfy DoR check 7 (>= 4 scenarios) that the original story failed, and it further bumps the story mtime. Pick one behavior; do not let generated amendments satisfy the DoR scenario count.

The rule 'if Section 8 already exists, preserve existing content and add Section 8.1' does not cover re-runs (stale or --force). A second run finds the 8.1 generated last time and adds another one, duplicating the table. Specify replacing an existing generated 8.1 section while keeping manual content.

Per-task plan files are named by sequential TASK-NNN. When a regeneration produces fewer tasks, the old task-plan-TASK-NNN files for the removed IDs stay on disk and look current. Delete existing task-plan-*-story-XXXX-YYYY.md files before regenerating.

The staleness check (0.3) compares mtime(story file) before 0.4 confirms the story file exists. It also ignores changes to the epic file and IMPLEMENTATION-MAP, both of which feed agent context, so plans built on an outdated epic or map are reused. Verify existence first and include the context inputs in the freshness comparison.

The anti-pattern 'Do NOT reorder RED before GREEN pairs (test-first is mandatory)' can be read as forbidding RED before GREEN, which is the opposite of what is meant. Reword to 'Never place a GREEN task before its RED counterpart'.

Rule 4 ('Tech Lead wins conflicts' with the Architect over implementation approaches) cannot trigger as specified. The Tech Lead prompt (lines 335-375) only produces VERIFY quality-gate tasks with no per-component approach, so there is nothing to compare against the Architect's proposals. Either have the TL emit per-component approach proposals or drop the rule.

The DoR pre-check looks for a `## Final Verdict` section, but x-story-plan never writes one. The DoR checklist it generates (x-story-plan SKILL.md ~778-830) puts the verdict under `## Summary` as `Verdict: **READY/NOT_READY**` and lists failures under `## Blockers`. The check will never find a verdict. Depending on how the agent reads that, it either skips the gate silently or does something undefined. `{failed_checks}` is also never mapped to a source; it should come from the Mandatory/Conditional checks table or the Blockers section. Nothing says what to do when a DoR file exists but its verdict is missing or malformed.

A NOT_READY story is set to BLOCKED but has no `blockedBy`. Resume Step 2 keeps any BLOCKED story with undefined `blockedBy` blocked forever, so a story stays stuck even after its DoR is fixed and re-planned to READY; `--resume` never re-runs the DoR check. Nothing says whether stories that depend on a DoR-blocked story get the block propagated to them, the way they would after a failure. The reason string also isn't stored in any checkpoint field.

The DoR path is hard-coded as `plans/epic-{epicId}/plans/...`. In the same change, x-story-plan now resolves suffixed epic dirs (`plans/epic-XXXX-*`) and writes DoR files there. For those epics the pre-check will report 'No DoR file found' and skip the gate silently.

No step writes per-task progress during execution. The only writer is x-dev-lifecycle Phase 8, which marks all tasks DONE once the story finishes; nothing records IN_PROGRESS, commitSha, or duration per task. If a story is interrupted mid-way, it has no `tasks` data, so Step 1b's task-level resume can never take effect. Also, the lifecycle subagent writes `execution-state.json` while the orchestrator updates the same file for parallel stories, which risks lost updates. Single-writer ownership needs to be defined.

The task `type` values here (DEV/TEST/SEC/REFACTOR) and the example agent mapping (architect doing DEV) don't match the task types x-story-plan emits (architecture/implementation/test/security/quality-gate/validation). That leaves the schema ambiguous for whoever fills it in.

PRE_PLANNED mode needs all 7 artifact types, with arch/tests/plan/security/compliance attributed to x-story-plan. x-story-plan's outputs are only tasks, task-plan-*, planning-report, and dor (its SKILL.md ~829-832); this change even makes the planning-report the primary evidence for architecture, tests, security, and plan. So x-story-plan output can never produce PRE_PLANNED; it always falls into HYBRID and regenerates planning. The architecture file name `architecture-story-*` also differs from the documented `arch-story-*` template output.

The mode table doesn't cover every case. If all 7 artifacts exist but some are stale, the PRE_PLANNED condition fails and the HYBRID condition ('some but not all exist') also fails, so no mode applies. HYBRID says to 'reuse existing fresh ones' but doesn't say what to do with stale ones.

The new `### Phase 0.5 — Planning Mode Detection` heading collides with the existing `## Phase 0.5 — API-First Contract Generation` right below it, and the phase overview at the top of the skill doesn't list it. Two phases share one number, which is ambiguous for an orchestrating agent.

The per-task status update sits after Phase 8 step 10 (`git checkout develop && git pull`). Editing the story file's Section 8.1 at that point changes the `develop` working tree after the PR is created and merged. That means either an uncommitted change or a direct commit to develop, which Rule 09 forbids, and the status update is never part of the story's PR. It also marks every task DONE at once, with no DoD/commit evidence and no handling of SKIPPED or failed tasks.

Task-by-task Phase 2 runs inline in the orchestrator instead of through the Phase 2 subagent, and it never invokes x-dev-implement's new task-aware mode. That leaves two separate definitions of the same loop. They already disagree: this one has no resume check or compile check, and its commit format is `[TDD:RED|GREEN|REFACTOR]` where x-dev-implement always uses `[TDD:GREEN]`.

The resume heuristic (the Implementation Guide's class exists and its tests pass, so the task is DONE) is unreliable. Tasks that modify an existing class get skipped wrongly because the file already exists and old tests pass. RED/test-only tasks can't be judged by 'tests pass'. The heuristic also ignores the task status and commitSha recorded in execution-state.json, which the epic-implement change claims are passed to this subagent.

Every task gets one combined commit, `feat(scope): implement TASK-NNN [TDD:GREEN]`, staging test and implementation together. That contradicts the test-first commit history required by the quality gates and the RED/GREEN/REFACTOR commits used elsewhere in this skill and in x-dev-lifecycle. It also labels test, security, and refactor tasks as `feat`, which breaks Conventional Commits-based version bumping.

The producer of the task artifacts is given inconsistently: here per-task plans come from `x-dev-lifecycle`, the integration notes say `x-lib-task-decomposer`, and x-dev-lifecycle says `x-story-plan Phase 4`. The '5. Mode determination' item is numbered as if it continues the earlier list, but it sits under a new subsection. 'Fresh' is used without a staleness rule.

'Task dependency not met → skip task' contradicts the dependency-ordered iteration in 2.5. Nothing says whether the skipped task is retried later, and there's no SKIPPED/BLOCKED status reported back. A skipped task can be silently left undone.

The EPIC_DIR resolution added in 0.2/0.3 isn't applied everywhere. Step 0.5 still checks and reports `plans/epic-XXXX/story-XXXX-YYYY.md`, so for suffixed epic dirs the story file is reported NOT_FOUND and planning aborts. Paths at ~173-176 and the output paths at ~536-702 and ~829-832 are also still hard-coded to `plans/epic-XXXX/`.

Of all the golden files, only java-quarkus/.claude x-dev-lifecycle was updated. About 69 other x-dev-lifecycle goldens (every profile, plus the .github/.codex/.agents variants) and every golden for x-dev-epic-implement, x-dev-implement, and x-story-plan were not regenerated. Golden-file tests will fail, which contradicts the PR description's claim that all existing tests pass. The PR also doesn't say whether the .github/codex skill sources need the same edits.

The guard checks the branch in the hook process's cwd, which is the orchestrator's (lead's) working directory, not the target implementer's branch. The process rules have implementers work on their own branches in separate worktrees, and the lead usually sits on `main`. In that setup the hook always hits the `main`/`master` early exit and allows the shutdown, so the main scenario it was written for is never guarded. If the lead happens to be on some other feature branch, it checks review evidence for the wrong branch. The hook needs to work out the target's branch, for example from the agent name, the team/task metadata, or the worktree list.

Review evidence is detected only by finding the sanitized branch name in a sidecar filename. Real review sidecars are named `${agent}--${contentHash}.json` (dev-team-review-gate.js:140,152), and the branch is stored in the JSON `branch` field (implement skill). So real sidecars never match, and when the branch check does run, every implementer shutdown is blocked until someone uses `--force-shutdown`. The merge gate handles this by reading `data.branch` first and only falling back to the filename. The guard should do the same.

`f.includes(sanitizedBranch)` is a substring match, so sidecars for `feat-12-foo` count as evidence for branch `feat/1`. That gives false 'reviewed' results. Compare the exact `branch` field instead, or use delimited filename matching.

Unlike the merge gate, which just gained symlink guards in #769, this hook doesn't lstat sidecars or skip symlinks and non-files. A symlinked or directory entry ending in `.json` counts as review evidence. The guard should apply the same validation as the merge gate.

The 'with review evidence' test makes a sidecar named `knuth--feat-123-test.json`, which the real review flow never produces (real names are `agent--<contentHash>.json`). The test passes only because the fixture matches the hook's wrong assumption, which hides the fact that real sidecars aren't recognized. There's also no test where the orchestrator is on `main` and the implementer is in a worktree, which is the realistic setup.

A string message counts as a shutdown request whenever it contains the substring `shutdown_request` anywhere. A normal message that just mentions the word to an implementer, such as 'don't send shutdown_request yet', gets blocked as a shutdown.

Every non-wrapper binary will fail this check. The heredoc is unquoted (`<<SH`), and in an unquoted heredoc a backslash only escapes `$`, `` ` `` and `\`. So `\"${binary}\"` keeps its backslashes, and the script sent to the container reads `binary_path="$(command -v \"jq\" || true)"`. Inside `$(...)`, `\"` is a literal quote character, so `command -v` looks up `"jq"` with the quotes included. That lookup always fails and the probe exits with `missing_binary:jq`. Check 3 then fails for jq, rg, ffmpeg, uv, gh and the rest, in both the gateway container and the sandbox image. The author's checks (`bash -n`, `git diff --check`) can't catch this. Use `command -v ${binary}` or `command -v "${binary}"` without the backslashes, and ideally quote the value with `shell_single_quote`/`%q`.

The expected binaries now come from the repo checkout (`scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json`), not from the manifest baked into the deployed image. The image manifest is only checked for existence and never read. When verify runs from a commit other than the one the image was built from, it checks the wrong set of binaries. A binary added to the repo manifest fails verify against an older image, and a binary dropped from the repo manifest is no longer checked even if the image still ships it. Before this change, verify read the manifest from inside the image. Read the image's manifest instead (for example `docker exec ... cat` it and parse it with jq on the runner), or at least compare it with the repo copy.

`runtime_wrapper_bin` now comes from `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN` in the verifier's own environment, defaulting to `/opt/daisy/bin`. The old probe read that variable inside the container, so it matched the image's actual configuration. If an image sets a different wrapper dir, verify now tests the wrong path. The wrapper existence test and the smoke test also each start a new `docker run` (in image mode), which means two extra container launches per wrapper binary.

The sandbox image probe used to run as `sh -lc` (a login shell). `build_target_shell_command` image mode now uses `sh -c`, so `/etc/profile` and profile.d PATH additions are no longer loaded. Binaries that are only on PATH in a login shell inside the sandbox image will now be reported as `missing_binary`. Agents in the sandbox likely run with a login environment, so this check no longer matches how they find binaries.

The `image` branch of `build_target_direct_exec_command` copies the smoke-suffix parsing, the metacharacter guard and the arg re-quoting from `build_direct_exec_smoke_command`, so a change to one copy can miss the other. The guard is also incomplete: `*'\\'*` inside single quotes matches two backslashes in a row, not one, so a single backslash gets past it. `%q` quoting still keeps this safe, but the guard doesn't do what it appears to.

Only InvalidOperationException is caught. When the SMTP server is unreachable, the TLS handshake fails, authentication is rejected or a recipient is refused, MailKit throws SocketException, SslHandshakeException, AuthenticationException or SmtpCommandException. These are not caught, so the user gets an unhandled 500. The `SendMailFailed` string was added to all four locales but is never used. Separately, several MailKit exceptions inherit from InvalidOperationException (ServiceNotConnectedException, ServiceNotAuthenticatedException). Those are reported as a 404 'Mailbox not found', which is misleading. Use a dedicated not-found result or exception type for the mailbox lookup, and map SMTP failures to a 502/500 with the `SendMailFailed` message.

Minimal APIs do not enforce DataAnnotations unless validation is registered (no AddValidation/validation filter exists in Program.cs). As a result, [Required], [StringLength], [MaxLength] and the ContentType regex are never checked on the server. A request with `To: null` causes a NullReferenceException at `request.To.Length` (500). A null Subject or Body passes straight to MimeKit. Any ContentType other than 'html' is silently sent as plain text. Validate these fields explicitly in the endpoint, or enable endpoint validation.
`request.To` is dereferenced with no null check. A JSON body that omits `to` or sets it to null crashes with a NullReferenceException and returns a 500 instead of a 400.

`ImapClient.GetFolder(SpecialFolder.Sent)` throws NotSupportedException when the server lacks SPECIAL-USE/XLIST. It does not return null in that case, so the `?? GetFoldersAsync(...)` fallback never runs. The exception is swallowed by the outer catch, which means on servers like GreenMail the message is never appended to Sent (the test plan expects it there). The fallback also only looks at top-level folders of the first namespace, so it misses names like `INBOX.Sent` or 'Sent Items'. It also never creates a Sent folder when none exists. Check `client.Capabilities` before calling GetFolder, or catch NotSupportedException and fall back.

Quill 2 renders bullet lists in `root.innerHTML` as `<ol><li data-list="bullet">`, and it expresses indent and alignment as `ql-*` CSS classes. HtmlSanitizer strips data-* attributes by default, and recipients do not have Quill's stylesheet. Result: bullet lists arrive as numbered lists and indentation is lost, and Turndown converts bullets to ordered lists too. Use `quill.getSemanticHTML()` instead of `root.innerHTML` so the output is portable for email.

`setHtml` writes `root.innerHTML` directly, bypassing Quill's model; Quill docs advise against this. The HTML comes from `marked.parse` without sanitization, so raw HTML in the markdown (e.g. ``) runs in the app origin. It is self-XSS today, but it becomes a real XSS once reply/forward prefill the body with received mail. Use `quill.clipboard.dangerouslyPasteHTML`, or `setContents(clipboard.convert(...))`, and sanitize the HTML (for example with DOMPurify) first.

Allowing the `data` scheme lets `<a href="data:text/html,...">` links through in outgoing mail. That is a common phishing and XSS vector, and recipient filters will score it as suspicious. Restrict data URIs to images, or drop the scheme.

When SmtpRequiresAuth is true but no password is stored, authentication is silently skipped. The send then fails later with a confusing server error. If SmtpUsername is null, AuthenticateAsync throws ArgumentNullException. Neither case produces a clear error.

HTML mail is sent as a single text/html part with no text/plain alternative. This hurts deliverability and spam scores, and degrades in text-only clients. Use BodyBuilder with both HtmlBody and TextBody.
Every recipient address is logged at Information level, which puts PII in persistent logs and telemetry (OpenTelemetry/Aspire). Log the recipient count, or log at Debug.
`error` is read from the response but never used. A server validation message, such as which address is invalid, is discarded and the user only sees a generic failure.

Every test replaces IMailSendingService with a mock, so the mailbox ownership check, MIME building, HTML sanitization and Sent-folder append in MailSendingService have no test coverage. The 'InvalidMailbox' test only checks that the mocked exception maps to a 404. It does not check that another user's mailbox is rejected.

`uv pip install -e '.[dev]'` installs no dev tooling. The project builds with hatchling from pyproject.toml, and pyproject.toml defines no `[project.optional-dependencies] dev` extra. The dev extras exist only in setup.py, which hatchling ignores. uv just warns that the extra is missing, so pytest, pytest-asyncio, black, mypy and ruff never get installed. Tests under tests/ (which need pytest and pytest-asyncio) and the README commands `pytest` / `mypy .` will fail in the container. Fix: add a `dev` extra to pyproject.toml or install from requirements-dev.in.

`workspaceFolder` is hardcoded to `/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus`, but there is no matching `workspaceMount`. The default mount is `/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}`, so any clone in a folder with another name (a fork rename, `git clone ... myfolder`, worktrees) opens a missing directory. postCreateCommand then runs in the wrong place and `python.defaultInterpreterPath` (line 21) points to a nonexistent venv. Use `/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}` in both places, or `${containerWorkspaceFolder}` for the interpreter path.
This interpreter path is hardcoded to the repository name, so it breaks the same way as `workspaceFolder` when the folder name differs. Use `${containerWorkspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python`.

The README says all dependencies install automatically and the OpenAPI proxy is reachable at localhost:8811. But the dev extra doesn't exist (see devcontainer.json:8), and nothing starts the proxy. The server also only reads a config file through the `PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG` env var, which the devcontainer never sets (no `containerEnv`). Following these steps leaves no running service and an unset config path. Document how to start the proxy (e.g. `start_openapi.sh` or `python -m proxmox_mcp.openapi_proxy`) and set `PROXMOX_MCP_CONFIG`, for example via `containerEnv`.

The build context is the repository root (`..`), but the Dockerfile copies nothing from it, and the repo has no .dockerignore. Every build sends the whole working tree to the Docker daemon, including any local `proxmox-config/config.json` with Proxmox API credentials and the `.venv`. Use `.devcontainer` as the context (the default) or add a .dockerignore.

The `python:3.11-slim` image is unpinned and `uv` (line 17) is installed without a version, so the 'reproducible' environment changes over time. Pin the uv version (and optionally the image digest), or use the official `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.11` image, which already has the vscode user and git.

Bean Validation ignores `@AssertTrue` on `fun harOppgittInntekt()`. Hibernate Validator only checks getter-style methods (`isX`/`getX`/`hasX`), and this method is not one. Because `arbeidstakerOgFrilansInntekt` is nullable, a request with no income still passes `@Valid`, gets journalført, and marks the task as solved with a null amount. Other DTOs in this codebase use `@get:AssertTrue val ...` or `fun isX()`. Use one of those forms here. There is also no non-negative check, so negative income is accepted.

Same problem as `OppgittInntekt`: `@AssertTrue` on `fun harOppgittInntekt()` is not a getter, so the validator never runs it. `AktivitetspengerInntektsrapporteringInnsending.valider()` also returns an empty list, so nothing on the server side enforces that income was reported.

The new `AKTIVITETSPENGER_INNTEKTRAPPORTERING` uses the placeholder brevkode `FIXME_AVP_INNTEKT_BREVKODE`, and the journalføring stream sends it to dokarkiv. Once this is deployed and the endpoint is reachable, every income report will be archived with an invalid brevkode, or journalføring will fail and the stream will get stuck retrying. Either set the real brevkode or keep the endpoint switched off until there is one.

The duplicate-check key is `personIdent_ytelse` with no task reference. If a user has several income-report tasks open, for example a backlog of months, they cannot submit a second report until the cache entry expires. Also, `markerOppgaveSomLøst` runs after `innsendingService.registrer`. If that call fails, the user gets an error even though the report is already on Kafka, the duplicate check blocks a retry, and the task stays unsolved. Include `oppgaveReferanse` in the key, and handle a failure to mark the task separately from the submission.

`hentInntektsrapporteringPeriode` only checks the task-data type. It does not check that the task is `RAPPORTER_INNTEKT` or still `ULØST`, so the same task can be reported again and journalført more than once after the duplicate cache expires.

The ACLs differ from the sibling topic files. Both `aktivitetspenger-soknad` and `ungdomsytelse-inntektsrapportering` give `ung-brukerdialog-api` read access on the mottatt and cleanup topics, but this file does not. If `ung-brukerdialog-api` consumes these events, as it does for the siblings, it will be denied. Please confirm the omission is intentional.

The controller test imports `InntektrapporteringUtils` from the ungdomsytelse package and posts an `UngdomsytelseInntektsrapportering` payload to the aktivitetspenger endpoint. It only passes because the two JSON shapes happen to match. Use the new `no.nav.brukerdialog.ytelse.aktivitetspenger.utils.InntektrapporteringUtils` instead. The test also stubs `barnService.hentBarn()`, which this flow never calls.
The template renders `{{ id }}`, but `AktivitetspengerInntektsrapporteringPdfData.pdfData()` never sets an `id` key, so this footer span is always empty.
`deltakelseId` is created and passed to `preprosessertSøknadSomJson`, but that function never uses it. This looks like dead code copied from the ungdomsytelse test.

Renaming a URL deletes its token. When the URL changes, the UI moves the '*' marker to the new URL key (McpServerGitSync.svelte ~L160-170). The backend then looks up `existingCred.Env[u]` under the new URL, finds nothing, and keeps no token. The old URL is no longer active, so its token is dropped too. The comment says a token is "transferred from a renamed one", but no code does this. Editing a private repo's URL (for example, to change the branch) silently removes its PAT, and the next sync fails. The request needs to say which old URL to carry the token over from (and the move should only be allowed between URLs on the same host).

Source URLs without a scheme are rewritten to start with `https://`, but the keys in `manifest.SourceURLCredentials` are left as typed. If an admin enters `gitlab.com/org/repo` with a token, the credential key never matches an active URL, so the token is skipped and never saved. Apply the same normalization to the credential keys.

The `GITHUB_AUTH_TOKEN` fallback now only applies when the URL exactly equals the hardcoded `https://github.com/obot-platform/mcp-catalog`. Before, it applied to every github.com URL. This breaks existing deployments that rely on the env var for private GitHub catalogs, including a custom `DefaultMCPCatalogPath`, which is added to SourceURLs automatically and has no way to store a per-URL token. Forms like `.../mcp-catalog.git` or a trailing slash also don't match. At minimum, compare against the configured `defaultCatalogPath`, and normalize the URL before comparing. Without a token, the unauthenticated GitHub size check is also limited to 60 requests per hour.

One shared `sizeLimitedFS` counts both the `.git` storage (packfile, index, temp files) and the checked-out working tree. Every byte is roughly counted twice: once compressed in the pack, then again uncompressed on checkout. So repos well under 100 MB can fail with 'repository too large'. This also disagrees with the GitHub API check, which measures repo size only. Count only object storage (or only the worktree), or adjust the limit to account for both.

`isGitRepoURL` now returns true for every gitlab.com URL. Raw-file catalog URLs that used to work, like `https://gitlab.com/org/repo/-/raw/main/catalog.json`, now go to `readGitCatalog`. `parseGitURL` then reads the branch as `-/raw/main/...`, which `validateBranchName` rejects because it starts with '-'. Existing GitLab raw-file catalog sources stop syncing. Paths containing `.git/`, like `example.com/x.git/raw/file.json`, are also misclassified the same way.

The catalog spec is saved before the credential is written or deleted. If `CreateCredential` or `DeleteCredential` fails, the API returns an error but the URL changes are already saved. That leaves URLs and tokens out of sync, for example a new private URL with no token. Write the credential first, or roll back the spec on failure.

`revealCatalogCredential` fetches the whole credential once per source URL on every sync, which is repeated round-trips to the credential store. If the store errors, the error is only logged and the sync goes ahead with no token. The user then sees an auth or clone error instead of the real cause. Fetch the credential once per sync, and record store errors in `SyncErrors`.

The temp directory is built from `skillset.name`, which comes straight from the remote manifest and is never validated. A name like `../../..` makes `tmpDir` resolve to `/` or any other directory. `safePath` checks paths against this already-escaped `tmpDir`, so it doesn't help. Together with manifest file entries that contain `..` (for example `rules: ['../../../home/u/.bashrc']`), a malicious skillset can write files anywhere the user has write access. Validate the name (e.g. `/^[a-z0-9._-]+$/` with no `..`) or check `tmpDir` against a fixed root.

`safePath` checks containment with `resolved.startsWith(baseDir)` and no trailing separator. With base `/tmp/spm/fsd`, a path that resolves to `/tmp/spm/fsd-evil/x` (e.g. `../fsd-evil/x`) passes the check. Use `path.relative` and reject results that start with `..` or are absolute, or compare against `baseDir + path.sep`.

Every entry is downloaded with `location.ref`, the default branch of the skillset's own repo. Cross-repo sources (`@owner/repo/path`) can point to a different repository whose default branch is not the same, e.g. `master` vs `main`. Those downloads get a 404 or come from the wrong ref. Resolve the ref per owner/repo, or carry a ref on each `FileEntry`.

`parseGitHubUrl` matches the branch in `/tree/<branch>/` but throws it away. `resolveIdentifier` then always uses the repo's default branch. So `https://github.com/org/repo/tree/develop/path` quietly installs from `main`, which is wrong code with no error. The test 'parses GitHub URL with non-main branch' only checks owner, repo and path, so it hides this. Return the ref from the parser and use it in `resolveIdentifier`.

The regex `tree/[^/]+/(.+)` assumes the branch name has no slashes. For a URL like `tree/feature/foo/claude/skill` it splits the branch and path in the wrong place. A trailing slash or `?query`/`#fragment` also ends up in the path.

Any source string that isn't `./` or `@` is now accepted as a repo-root path, including typos and full URLs like `https://example.com/skill`. These used to fail with a clear error; now they become broken GitHub paths and fail later with confusing 404s. The resolver also never produces the `url` or `local` download sources, so the URL and local download support described in the PR can't actually be reached from `spm install`.

The `..` check only covers bare-path sources. `./` sources, the `files` entries, `setup` and the agents/rules/hooks lists are joined without any check. The `includes('..')` test is also wrong in the other direction: it rejects valid names such as `foo..bar`. Normalize and check path segments in one consistent place.

The PR description says files go to `.tmp/<skillset-name>/`, but the code writes to the OS temp dir (`os.tmpdir()/spm/<name>`). That is a fixed, predictable shared path on multi-user systems, and it is not cleaned between runs, so stale files from earlier installs pile up.

All files are fetched at once with an unbounded `Promise.all`. A large skillset fires many parallel requests at raw.githubusercontent, and if one fails the rest keep running in the background. Consider limiting concurrency.

`vi.restoreAllMocks()` does not undo `vi.stubGlobal`, so the stubbed `fetch` can leak into other tests. Use `vi.unstubAllGlobals()`. The same problem is in `download-from-github.test.ts` and `download-from-url.test.ts`.

The PR commits a project-level `.spmrc.yml` to the repo root. It looks like a local dev or test artifact (probably so `readConfig` passes in the integration test). If that's the reason, it should be a fixture rather than repository config.

The new `agent-app` Application tracks the feature branch `AI-20-AISecureAgent-Feature-collection`. Every other app tracks `HEAD` or a pinned version. Once this merges, production follows an unreviewed feature branch, so changes pushed there deploy automatically (automated sync with prune/selfHeal). If the branch is deleted after merge, the app breaks and can't sync. Use `HEAD` or a release tag.

The container has no `envFrom: secretRef: ms-secret-vault`, which the shared chart injected into every service. The configmap sets MySQL (`admin_db`, user `root`), Kafka and Redis connection details but no password, so credentials must have come from that Vault-backed secret. Without it the service will likely fail to connect to MySQL and other middleware.

The liveness/readiness probes (`/ai-secure-agent-ms/v1/ping`) were dropped in the move. Kubernetes will send traffic to the pod before it is ready and won't restart it if it hangs, which is worse than the chart-based setup.

The resource requests/limits (100m/256Mi requests, 200m/345Mi limits) were dropped. The pod now runs unbounded (BestEffort QoS), so it can starve neighbours or be evicted first, and an HPA based on utilisation can't work. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` is still set, which suggests memory was a known concern.

The pod annotation `linkerd.io/inject: disabled` was dropped. If the default namespace or cluster has Linkerd auto-injection on, this pod now gets a sidecar, which changes networking and resource use without anyone intending it.

The `applogs` hostPath volume (`/tmp/logs/ai-secure-agent-ms` mounted at `/app/logs`) and its fix-perm init container were dropped. If the app writes logs to `/app/logs`, they no longer reach the host path that log collection (log-ms) reads, and writes may fail if the directory doesn't exist or isn't writable.
